```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
scores <- read.csv("compare-data/scores.csv")
densities <- read.csv("compare-data/densities.csv")
settings <- read.csv("compare-data/settings.csv")
methods <- c("uncorrected", "paired", "bridgenorm", "CytoNorm", "cyCombine")
colours <- c(uncorrected = "grey55", paired = "#0072B2", bridgenorm = "#D55E00", CytoNorm = "#56B4E9",
  cyCombine = "#009E73")
scenarios <- expand.grid(design = c("balanced", "confounded"), batch_effect = c("global", "state"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)[, 2:1]
scenario_title <- function(be, de) {
  paste0(if (be == "global") "Global shift" else "State-specific", ", ", de)
}
scores$ratio <- scores$effect / scores$effect_true
mean_of <- function(value, be, de, m) {
  round(mean(scores[[value]][scores$batch_effect == be & scores$design == de & scores$method == m]), 3)
}
range_of <- function(value, be, de, m) {
  v <- scores[[value]][scores$batch_effect == be & scores$design == de & scores$method == m]
  paste(sprintf("%.2f", range(v)), collapse = " to ")
}
```

This article compares bridgenorm with two widely used batch-correction tools, [CytoNorm](https://github.com/saeyslab/CytoNorm) and [cyCombine](https://github.com/biosurf/cyCombine), on simulated data where the truth is known. The methods were run once with the script `tools/sim-compare.R` in the package repository; the article reads its saved results, so building it does not need CytoNorm or cyCombine.

## Simulated data

Each simulated data set has four batches. Batch b1 is the anchor and carries no batch effect. Every batch holds two bridge aliquots from one reference donor and eight study samples from different donors. Cells come from four populations and are measured on six markers. Study donors differ a little in population mix and marker levels. Cases carry a known condition effect: +0.6 on marker M4 in population C.

Two kinds of batch effect are simulated:

- **Global shift**: one shift per batch and marker, the same for every cell.
- **State-specific shift and scale**: a shift and a stretch or compression per batch, population and marker, so the batch effect differs between cell states and changes the shape of the distributions.

And two study designs:

- **Balanced**: four cases and four controls in every batch.
- **Confounded**: 1, 2, 6 and 7 cases in batches b1 to b4, so condition and batch overlap.

That makes four scenarios, each simulated with three seeds.

```{r settings}
knitr::kable(settings, col.names = c("Setting", "Value"))
```

## Methods and settings

All methods use the same 5 by 5 self-organising map grid. bridgenorm and CytoNorm are fitted on the first bridge aliquot of every batch; the second aliquot is held out for scoring. cyCombine has no separate apply step; it is fitted on and corrects all cells, study samples included, as it is designed to. CytoNorm uses 10 metaclusters, because its default of 30 exceeds the 25 map nodes. The paired shift (`bn_fit_paired()`, one shift per batch and marker) is the baseline.

## How the methods are scored

- **Held-out bridge EMD** measures how much batch effect is left. The held-out bridge aliquot is the same donor in every batch, so after a perfect correction its distributions match across batches. Per marker, the score takes the largest one-dimensional earth mover's distance between any two batches, then the median over markers. Lower is better. With 1,500 cells per aliquot, sampling noise alone keeps the score above zero; the best methods level off near 0.05.
- **Condition effect recovery** measures whether biology survives. Per study sample, the median of M4 in population C cells is taken; the effect is the mean of cases minus the mean of controls, with no batch term. The plot shows the estimate divided by the true +0.6, so 1 means the effect is kept.

## Batch effect left after correction

```{r emd, fig.height = 5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 7.5, 2.5, 1), cex = 0.75)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(scenarios))) {
  be <- scenarios$batch_effect[i]
  de <- scenarios$design[i]
  d <- scores[scores$batch_effect == be & scores$design == de, ]
  y <- match(d$method, methods)
  plot(d$heldout_emd, y, xlim = c(0, max(scores$heldout_emd)), ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), yaxt = "n",
    pch = 19, col = colours[d$method], xlab = "", ylab = "", main = scenario_title(be, de))
  axis(2, at = seq_along(methods), labels = methods, las = 1)
  means <- tapply(d$heldout_emd, factor(d$method, levels = methods), mean)
  segments(means, seq_along(methods) - 0.3, means, seq_along(methods) + 0.3, lwd = 2)
  mtext("Held-out bridge EMD (lower is better)", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.7)
}
par(op)
```

Points are the three simulation seeds; bars are their mean. The design (balanced or confounded) only changes the study samples, so the bridge scores repeat across the two designs.

**Global shift.** bridgenorm (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "global", "balanced", "bridgenorm")`), the paired shift (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "global", "balanced", "paired")`) and cyCombine (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "global", "balanced", "cyCombine")`) bring the held-out EMD down from `r mean_of("heldout_emd", "global", "balanced", "uncorrected")` to the level where they can no longer be told apart. CytoNorm leaves more (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "global", "balanced", "CytoNorm")`). CytoNorm clusters cells on the same markers that carry the shift, so in this simulation its clusters likely split by batch, and several of its clusters held fewer than 50 bridge cells in some batches, which CytoNorm leaves unnormalised. bridgenorm avoids the first problem by shifting cells globally before it builds its map. With more bridge cells, or with clustering markers that carry little batch effect, CytoNorm would likely do better.

**State-specific shift and scale.** No method removes this batch effect fully. cyCombine (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "state", "balanced", "cyCombine")`) and bridgenorm (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "state", "balanced", "bridgenorm")`) leave the least, ahead of CytoNorm (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "state", "balanced", "CytoNorm")`) and the paired shift (`r mean_of("heldout_emd", "state", "balanced", "paired")`). Each bridge aliquot here has only 1,500 cells, about 60 per map node. With the default `shrink_k = 300`, a node keeps only about a sixth of its own quantile curve and borrows the rest from the batch-wide curve, so much of the state-specific part is not corrected. Larger bridge samples, or a smaller `shrink_k`, give each node more weight.

## Biology kept after correction

```{r effect, fig.height = 5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 7.5, 2.5, 1), cex = 0.75)
lim <- range(c(0.4, scores$ratio))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(scenarios))) {
  be <- scenarios$batch_effect[i]
  de <- scenarios$design[i]
  d <- scores[scores$batch_effect == be & scores$design == de, ]
  y <- match(d$method, methods)
  plot(d$ratio, y, xlim = lim, ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), yaxt = "n", pch = 19, col = colours[d$method],
    xlab = "", ylab = "", main = scenario_title(be, de))
  abline(v = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
  axis(2, at = seq_along(methods), labels = methods, las = 1)
  mtext("Estimated / true condition effect (1 = kept)", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.7)
}
par(op)
```

**Balanced design.** All methods give estimates close to those of the uncorrected data. With condition balanced within batch, a batch effect does not bias the case–control difference much. Under the state-specific batch effect, every estimate sits above 1, uncorrected included: the batches that stretch M4 in population C also stretch the condition effect, and no method fully undoes the stretch.

**Confounded design.** Here a batch effect left in the data biases the estimate, because cases sit mostly in some batches. Uncorrected data range from `r range_of("ratio", "global", "confounded", "uncorrected")` of the true effect under the global shift. bridgenorm stays close to the truth (`r range_of("ratio", "global", "confounded", "bridgenorm")`), as does the paired shift. cyCombine varies more (`r range_of("ratio", "global", "confounded", "cyCombine")`): it is fitted on the study samples, so part of the condition effect, which differs between batches, can be removed as batch effect. CytoNorm (`r range_of("ratio", "global", "confounded", "CytoNorm")`) varies most, in line with the batch effect it leaves. Under the state-specific batch effect, every method varies widely in the confounded design, bridgenorm included (`r range_of("ratio", "state", "confounded", "bridgenorm")`), because no method removes that batch effect fully. With three seeds per scenario, these ranges are rough.

## What the correction looks like

The density of marker M4 in population C cells of the held-out bridge aliquot, seed 1, balanced design. After a good correction, the four batches overlap.

```{r densities, fig.height = 4.6}
batch_colours <- c(b1 = "black", b2 = "#E69F00", b3 = "#0072B2", b4 = "#CC79A7")
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 5), mar = c(2.5, 2, 2.5, 0.5), cex = 0.6)
for (be in c("global", "state")) {
  for (m in methods) {
    d <- densities[densities$batch_effect == be & densities$design == "balanced" & densities$method == m, ]
    dens <- lapply(split(d$value, d$batch), density)
    plot(NULL, xlim = range(d$value), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(dens, function(x) max(x$y)))),
      main = paste0(m, "\n", if (be == "global") "global shift" else "state-specific"), xlab = "",
      ylab = "", yaxt = "n")
    for (b in names(dens)) lines(dens[[b]], col = batch_colours[[b]], lwd = 1.5)
  }
}
legend("topright", legend = names(batch_colours), col = batch_colours, lwd = 1.5, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## Limits of this comparison

- The simulation was written by the bridgenorm author and follows bridgenorm's design: one reference donor in every batch, batch b1 free of batch effect. Its batch effects are simple shifts and linear stretches.
- The bridge samples are small (1,500 cells per aliquot), which limits bridgenorm's node curves and CytoNorm's clusters alike. Real bridge samples are often larger.
- Each method ran with one setting per tool. CytoNorm in particular depends on which markers it clusters on; it clustered on all six here.
- cyCombine and bridgenorm answer different questions. cyCombine removes differences between batches of all cells; bridgenorm removes only what the bridge samples show. Which is right depends on whether biology can differ between batches.
